piece.title: String Quartet No.12 in F major, Op.96 (“American”)
piece.why: Pretty and clear, then a handoff: Violin I sings the theme, then the cello takes it over while Violin I drops to the repeated-note accompaniment on top.

roster.label: Church brass: 2 trumpets (one beginner), horn, euphonium

plan.summary: This is a lyrical 6/8 piece in D minor. Violin 1 has the tune until bar 12, the cello answers it in canon in bars 10–12, and the cello takes the tune over from bar 13. Trumpet 1 plays the tune the whole way through. The horn plays the moving accompaniment and the euphonium holds the bass, so the melody always sits clearly above a warm brass bed. The beginner trumpet plays the short canon answer, which stays in an easy range.

assignments.reason: Main tune. Played an octave lower (about A3–A4) because the violin part goes up to A5. It stays above the euphonium bass, and the trumpet's bright sound carries it over the horn.
The cello takes the tune here in the same register (A3–A4). Trumpet 1 follows it, so the melody stays with one player.
The cello's canon answer to the tune. It sits between A3 and A4, an easy range for the beginner, and gives a clear, exposed entrance.
The viola's rippling arpeggios (F3–D4) as written. With the euphonium bass now back at its written pitch, the horn sits above it and below the tune.

Violin 1's repeated-note accompaniment, an octave down (C4–C5). This fits the horn's range, and its soft tone stays apart from the trumpet tune. It replaces the Violin 2 part, which would have dropped below the bass.
Cello bass line at written pitch (A2–A3), so it stays at the bottom, under the horn and the trumpet.
Bar 9 of the bass line. Using the upper note of the cello's double stop skips the low C2, which the euphonium can't play, so the bass stays at written pitch.
When the cello moves up to the canon and then the tune, the viola becomes the lowest part. The euphonium follows it to keep the bass at the bottom.

dropped.reason: Repeated-note filler with the same harmony as the arpeggios. Played an octave down, it would cross the tune or drop below the bass. At written pitch it goes above the horn's range, and no other player is free.
